items.stem: What does a weighted graph consist of?
options: A table of records
A list of values in order
A tree with a single root only
Nodes (vertices) joined by edges that have a value (weight) such as distance or cost
items.answer: Nodes (vertices) joined by edges that have a value (weight) such as distance or cost
items.markingKey: Used in AI to model maps, networks and states.

items.stem: Explain why A* usually explores fewer nodes than Dijkstra's algorithm.
items.answer: The heuristic guides the search towards the goal, so nodes that lead away from the goal are less likely to be expanded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why the heuristic used by A* must not overestimate the remaining distance.
items.answer: If it overestimates, a shorter path may be ignored, so A* may not return the optimal (shortest) path.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Jonas is programming a game character that must find its way around a map for MetroBus. (a) Explain why a graph is a suitable way to represent the map. (b) Suggest a suitable heuristic and explain why it is admissible.
items.answer: (a) Locations as nodes, paths as edges with weights (distance/time); algorithms can then compute optimal routes. (b) Straight-line (Euclidean) distance: a path along edges can never be shorter than a straight line, so it never overestimates.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark heuristic; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A navigation app developed in Jakarta plans routes between landmarks. (a) Explain how A* uses a heuristic to improve the search. (b) Suggest a suitable heuristic and explain why it is admissible.
items.answer: (a) Chooses node with lowest f = g + h; h estimates distance to goal (e.g. straight line), so search heads towards goal, expanding fewer nodes. (b) Straight-line (Euclidean) distance: a path along edges can never be shorter than a straight line, so it never overestimates.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3] (b) 1 mark heuristic; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: What does Dijkstra's algorithm find?
options: The shortest path from a start node to every other node in a weighted graph
The minimum number of edges
The longest path
A path that visits every node once
items.answer: The shortest path from a start node to every other node in a weighted graph
items.markingKey: It repeatedly visits the unvisited node with the smallest known distance.

items.stem: How does A* differ from Dijkstra's algorithm?
options: It ignores the edge weights
It only works on unweighted graphs
It always explores every node
It adds a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to the goal to choose which node to explore
items.answer: It adds a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to the goal to choose which node to explore
items.markingKey: f(n) = g(n) + h(n).

items.stem: What is machine learning?
options: Programming every rule by hand
Storing large amounts of data
A type of computer hardware
A branch of AI in which a system learns from data and improves its performance without being explicitly programmed for every case
items.answer: A branch of AI in which a system learns from data and improves its performance without being explicitly programmed for every case
items.markingKey: Models are trained on data.

items.stem: Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning.
items.answer: Supervised learning is trained on labelled data with known outputs to predict labels; unsupervised learning finds patterns/clusters in unlabelled data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a large amount of training data is needed in machine learning.
items.answer: More (representative) examples let the model generalise to new data and reduce errors/overfitting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Which type of machine learning is used when a game-playing AI improves by playing millions of games against itself and being rewarded for wins?
options: Unsupervised learning
Rule-based expert system
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
items.answer: Reinforcement learning
items.markingKey: reinforcement: rewards and penalties.

items.stem: Identify the type of machine learning used when a robot learns to walk by receiving a reward each time it moves forward without falling. Justify your answer.
items.answer: Reinforcement learning: the system learns by trial and error from rewards and penalties.
items.markingKey: 1 mark type; 1 mark justification [2]

items.stem: Lakeside College in Mumbai wants to use machine learning to improve its services. (a) Explain one ethical issue of using machine learning in this way. (b) Compare reinforcement learning with supervised learning.
items.answer: (a) Bias in training data may lead to unfair decisions; lack of transparency about how decisions are made; privacy of personal data. (b) Reinforcement: no labelled data, learns from rewards through trial and error; supervised: learns from labelled examples.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark issue; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Supervised learning uses which kind of training data?
options: Unlabelled data
Labelled data, where the correct output is known for each input
Rewards and penalties only
No data at all
items.answer: Labelled data, where the correct output is known for each input
items.markingKey: The model learns to map inputs to the given labels.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is machine learning? (b) Supervised learning uses which kind of training data?
items.answer: (a) A branch of AI in which a system learns from data and improves its performance without being explicitly programmed for every case (b) Labelled data, where the correct output is known for each input
items.markingKey: (a) Models are trained on data. (b) The model learns to map inputs to the given labels.

A is true but R is false

options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Rule-based expert system
Reinforcement learning
items.answer: Supervised learning
items.markingKey: supervised: labelled training data.

items.stem: Starlight Cinemas tests a supervised learning model on 259 labelled examples. It correctly identifies 83 positive and 147 negative cases; it misses 17 positive cases and wrongly flags 12 negative cases as positive. Calculate the accuracy as a percentage and explain why more training data might improve it.
items.answer: 230 ÷ 259 × 100 = 88.8%; more varied labelled data helps the model generalise to new cases.
items.markingKey: correct = 230 (1); accuracy 88.8% (1); explanation (1) [3]

items.stem: MetroBus in Seoul wants to automate some decisions. Assess the use of machine learning by MetroBus to make decisions about its customers.
items.answer: Points in favour: fast, consistent decisions on large data; can find patterns humans miss; improves over time. Points against / limitations: bias in training data; decisions hard to explain; privacy concerns; need for large labelled data sets; errors may harm individuals. Conclusion: use with human oversight, transparent models and audited data.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. items.stem: Nova Telecom in Istanbul wants to use machine learning to improve its services. (a) Describe how a supervised learning model is trained and tested. (b) Explain one ethical issue of using machine learning in this way.
items.answer: (a) Labelled data split into training and test sets; model learns from training data; accuracy measured on unseen test data; adjust and repeat. (b) Bias in training data may lead to unfair decisions; lack of transparency about how decisions are made; privacy of personal data.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 3 [3] (b) 1 mark issue; 1 mark explanation [2]

items.stem: What is an artificial neural network?
options: A type of search algorithm
A network of connected nodes (neurons) in layers, with weighted connections, modelled on the brain
A network of computers in a LAN
A database of facts
items.answer: A network of connected nodes (neurons) in layers, with weighted connections, modelled on the brain
items.markingKey: Input layer, hidden layer(s), output layer.

items.stem: Explain how a neural network learns using back propagation.
items.answer: Inputs pass forward to give an output; the error (actual − expected) is calculated; the error is propagated back and weights adjusted to reduce it; repeated over many examples.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 3 [3]

items.stem: Explain why deep learning needs large amounts of data and processing power.
items.answer: Many layers and weights must be adjusted; many examples are needed to learn features without overfitting; training uses many calculations (GPUs).

items.answer: sum = -0.2; output = 0

items.stem: Aisha is advising MetroBus on AI. Assess the use of machine learning by MetroBus to make decisions about its customers.
items.answer: Points in favour: fast, consistent decisions on large data; can find patterns humans miss; improves over time. Points against / limitations: bias in training data; decisions hard to explain; privacy concerns; need for large labelled data sets; errors may harm individuals. Conclusion: use with human oversight, transparent models and audited data.
items.markingKey: Up to 4 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 4 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion.
